In a standard eager execution model, every kernel launch requires the CPU to prepare command descriptors, manage memory buffers, and send commands to the GPU via the driver API. This process involves significant system call overhead, context switching, and potential stalls, which become critical bottlenecks when executing thousands of small kernels (a common scenario in deep learning training loops). By contrast, a CUDA graph captures the dependency structure and parameters of these kernels into a static DAG on the GPU. Once captured, the entire graph can be instantiated and launched with a single API call, drastically reducing the CPU workload to a simple "play" command and allowing the GPU to execute the sequence with minimal latency and higher throughput.

Replaying a CUDA graph is faster than launching the same kernels eagerly primarily because it eliminates the significant CPU overhead associated with individual kernel launches. In an eager execution model, every kernel invocation requires the CPU to prepare arguments, perform validation, and issue a command to the GPU driver to enqueue the operation into the hardware queue. This process involves multiple function calls, memory copies, and synchronization checks that consume considerable CPU cycles. In contrast, a CUDA graph captures a sequence of kernels and their dependencies into a single static data structure. When this graph is replayed, the CPU only needs to issue a single command to the GPU to execute the entire pre-compiled sequence. This drastic reduction in CPU-to-GPU communication allows the CPU to get out of the way, which is particularly beneficial for small kernels or deep layers where the launch overhead can dominate the actual computation time.

When kernels are launched eagerly, the GPU’s command processor handles each kernel as a separate event, potentially introducing gaps in execution as it processes the queue. Eager kernel launching involves significant CPU-side overhead for every individual kernel invocation. When launching kernels one by one, the CPU must execute host code to validate arguments, update the CUDA stream state, and issue the command to the GPU driver, which then translates this into hardware packets. In scenarios with many small kernels or complex dependency graphs, this "launch latency" and the resulting idle bubbles on the GPU between kernels can become a bottleneck, as the GPU finishes executing a kernel before the CPU has finished issuing the next one.

A CUDA graph mitigates this by allowing the entire sequence of kernel launches and data transfers to be captured once and recorded as a single, static Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) in device memory. During replay, the CPU issues a single command to execute the entire graph, rather than thousands of individual commands. This drastically reduces the CPU overhead and allows the GPU’s work scheduler to look ahead, potentially overlapping the execution of independent kernels or memory copies more efficiently. The result is a tighter pipeline where the GPU remains busy with minimal gaps, leading to lower end-to-end latency, especially for inference workloads or iterative loops with fixed structures.
